Product Id: Hate crimes refer to criminal offences committed against a person or property that is motivated in whole or in part by bias, prejudice or hate based on race, national or ethnic origin, language, colour, religion, sex, age, mental or physical disability, sexual orientation or gender identity or expression, or on any other similar factor. For more information on the concepts, methods and quality of the data contained in this table, consult the statistical data documentation: Uniform Crime Reporting Survey - 3302.

Data coverage for police-reported data varies slightly each year. Hate crime data for 2025 covers 99.6% of the Canadian population. Coverage for each province/territory is virtually 100% with the exception of New Brunswick (90.9%) due to the exclusion of Saint John Police Force. These percentages are based on police-reported data and populations for the 2025 data cycle.

Over the past two decades, police services across Canada have continued to advance their identification and reporting of hate crime incidents. Changes in reporting practices can have an effect on hate crime statistics. For example, an increase in the number of hate crime incidents reported can be influenced by the introduction of a hate crime awareness campaign.

Data submitted through the Uniform Crime Reporting Survey (UCR) 2.1 supplemental survey for Saint John and Québec police services for 2014 and 2015, and Calgary Police Service for 2014-2016, does not contain detailed motivation information. As such, these data fall into the unknown category.
Other sex or gender includes unknown sex or gender and motivation against intersex, transgender and agender.

Excluded from this table are the small number of police services that do not report to the Uniform Crime Reporting Survey (UCR) 2. With the exception of Lasalle Police Service, Kahnawake Mohawk Peacekeepers, Six Nations Police Service and Dalmeny Police Service  in 2017, who provided data through special submission.

Hate crime, organized crime and cybercrime data from the Uniform Crime Reporting (UCR) Survey are now revised back one year with each annual release. This approach was introduced for the 2019 data release and was applied to the 2018 revised data.

Police data on hate crimes reflect only the incidents that come to the attention of police and are classified as hate crimes. Hate crime incident counts include both confirmed and suspected hate crime incidents.

Under the authority of the Canadian Forces Provost Marshal (CFPM), the Canadian Forces Military Police Group (CF MP Gp) is now reporting incidents to the Uniform Crime Reporting (UCR) Survey. They have provided incidents going back to January 2020 and are not included in 2025.  Data from the CFPM are aggregated at the national level. Therefore, regional totals will not equal Canada-level totals.
Selected data at the regional level have been suppressed due to small counts and to protect confidentiality.

Starting in 2023, data for new expanded coding options for the hate crime type and motivation variables, introduced in version 2.4 of the Uniform Crime Reporting (UCR) Survey, are available from some police service respondents. Police services not yet reporting the new options will begin using them as soon as their Records Management System (RMS) allows it.

The increase in hate crime incidents observed beginning in 2023 can be attributed, in part, to the establishment of a dedicated hate crimes unit in Halifax resulting in higher reporting and increased public awareness. For more information visit: https://humanrights.novascotia.ca/news-events/events/understanding-hate-crimes

In 2025, there was a notable increase in police-reported hate crimes targeting the South Asian population, particularly in Ontario and British Columbia. Because this increase went against the broader declining trend for most other racialized or ethnic groups, it contributed to the overall stability in hate crimes targeting race or ethnicity. Annual changes in police-reported hate crime may reflect changes in reporting, identification by police, local context and investigative practices, as well as changes in the occurrence of hate-motivated crime.
